\section{The forecast and its presentation to Parliament}
\label{sec:lttv-forecast}

In March 2015 the CRTC told television distributors to offer, by March 2016, an entry-level service \enquote{priced at no more than \$25 (not including equipment) per month} \citep[para.~26]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. Every discretionary channel was to be available on its own or in small packages by March 2016, and in both forms by December 2016 \citep[para.~47]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. The policy came out of the \textit{Let's Talk TV} proceeding, at which, by one later account, \enquote{virtually all parties expressed concerns about potential impacts of unbundling} \citep[para.~xxii, p.~5]{nordicity2015television}.

Nordicity and Peter Miller's \textit{Canadian Television 2020}, dated December 2015, was prepared for ACTRA (the Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists), the Canadian Media Guild, the Directors Guild of Canada, Friends of Canadian Broadcasting and Unifor. It modelled two worlds from 2015 to 2020: a baseline with \enquote{technological and consumer behaviour changes, assuming that the pre-existing broadcasting regulatory regime remains}, and the same world with the CRTC's decisions overlaid \citep[para.~ii, p.~1]{nordicity2015television}. I call these the report's baseline and its reform scenario; the forecast is the gap between them, and a quantity's path under the reform scenario is its reform path. A third scenario, with the decisions modified, isn't checked here.

By 2020, the report concluded, the decisions were \enquote{likely to result in a loss of 15,130 FTEs of employment in the Canadian economy}, counted in full-time equivalents (FTEs), along with \$\lttvGDPTotal{} million of GDP. Of those jobs, \lttvJobsDirect{} were directly in broadcasting and production and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} were spin-off employment, the indirect and induced employment in other sectors \citep[para.~xliv and Table~1 with its note, p.~12]{nordicity2015television}. The report also divides the total by the sector whose losses give rise to it: \lttvFTEProd{} to independent production (\lttvFTEProdDirect{} direct, \lttvFTEProdSpin{} spin-off) and \lttvFTEBroadcast{} to broadcasting (\lttvFTEBroadcastDirect{} direct, \lttvFTEBroadcastSpin{} spin-off), as table~\ref{tab:jobs-reconciliation} sets out \citep[paras.~246, 248, 250; Tables~22--23, pp.~90--92]{nordicity2015television}. The \lttvFTESpecProd{} (\lttvFTESpecProdShare{}) attributed to production and, within broadcasting, to specialty and pay services depend in the model on those services' revenue and on spending on Canadian programming, which is why specialty and pay revenue is the main test below.

The job and GDP figures sit at the end of a chain. Subscribers move to cheaper unbundled packages; distributors lose retail revenue and pass most of the loss to Canadian channels as lower wholesale fees; weaker channels close; spending on Canadian programming falls; and input-output multipliers turn the spending into jobs and GDP. The report links these estimates to reductions in broadcasting revenue and production financing \citep[para.~245]{nordicity2015television}, and I found no offset in it for the spending that subscribers who pay less redirect elsewhere. The report states the assumptions that drive each link. Subscribers taking the entry-level package with chosen channels, which the report calls Build Your Own Package (BYOP), make up \lttvByopSixteen{} of all subscribers in 2016, \lttvByopSeventeen{} in 2017 and \lttvByopEighteen{} from 2018 \citep[para.~202, Table~18, p.~76]{nordicity2015television}; I call this the report's BYOP uptake. Distributors attribute \lttvReportCanShare{} of the retail revenue they lose to Canadian services and pass \lttvReportPassThrough{} of that part on to them as lower wholesale fees \citep[paras.~206--207, p.~77]{nordicity2015television}. By 2020, \lttvReportClosuresVI{} of the Category A and B specialty channels owned by the large vertically integrated companies, which own both distributors and channels, close, and \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} of the independents' \citep[paras.~232--233, p.~85]{nordicity2015television}; the report's footnote 31, citing the CRTC, names the English-language vertically integrated entities as Bell, Rogers and Shaw/Corus.

By 2020 the reform path runs \$\lttvSpecImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvSpecShareTwenty{}) a year below the baseline for the revenue of specialty and pay services (\enquote{channels}, for short, below) and \$\lttvBDUImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvBDUShareTwenty{}) below it for distributors' revenue \citep[paras.~xxvi--xxvii]{nordicity2015television}. Canadian programming expenditure (CPE), which in the report includes distributors' contributions as well as programming services' spending, runs \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million below.

The report divides the revenue shortfall into four components: unbundling; the change from requiring a preponderance of Canadian channels among those each subscriber receives to among those offered, with the end of access rules, which it models as Canadian channels' share of BYOP subscribers' wholesale fees falling from \lttvPrepFrom{} to \lttvPrepTo{} by 2020 \citep[para.~212]{nordicity2015television}; an exemption order under which streaming services such as Crave TV and Shomi, until then offered only to TV subscribers, could compete for all viewers, which it expected to \enquote{materially increase cord cutting and cord shaving} \citep[para.~xxiii]{nordicity2015television}, that is, cancellations and downgrades of TV subscriptions; and channel closures \citep[Figs.~2--3]{nordicity2015television}.

Unbundling and the preponderance change act through BYOP subscribers and so scale with uptake; the report sets the exemption order and closures separately, though it values them partly from the other two \citep[paras.~220, 234]{nordicity2015television}.

\subsection{What the committee heard}

On 12 April 2016 Ian Morrison of Friends of Canadian Broadcasting, accompanied by Miller, put the report to the Commons Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage. Its key findings, he said, were that \enquote{by 2020, some 15,130 media jobs will be lost}, along with \enquote{a \$400-million drop in Canadian program expenditures} that was \enquote{18\% of what now exists}, \enquote{all of this as the direct result of Let's Talk TV regulatory changes}. He added that the authors had \enquote{advanced proposals to reduce the negative impact of the CRTC's decisions by as much as 75\%} \citep[time marks 0900--0905]{commons2016chpc8}.

Two of these phrases depart from the report. The \lttvJobsTotal{} FTEs are economy-wide, and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} of them are spin-off employment in other sectors, so \enquote{media jobs} misdescribes them; and the report describes its \lttvCPEShareStated{} as a share of projected 2020 baseline spending, not of current spending. The \$400 million rounds the report's \$399 million, and \enquote{direct result} attributes the losses to the decisions, as the report does, though \enquote{will be lost} is firmer than the report's \enquote{likely}. The 18\% itself is the report's, though its figures don't reproduce it: its baseline puts 2020 CPE at \$\lttvCPEBaselineTwenty{} million, so its \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million reduction is \lttvCPEShareTwenty{} of baseline, not the \lttvCPEShareStated{} its text states \citep[para.~239; Figs.~8, 9, 43]{nordicity2015television}. Against the report's own forecast for 2015, the reduction is \lttvCPEShareFifteen{}, and against what existed when Morrison spoke, the CRTC's count of 2015 spending (\$\lttvCPECRTCFifteen{} million), it's \lttvCPEShareCRTCFifteen{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016}. None of the \lttvCPENCandidates{} shares tested, built from the report's figures over \lttvCPENDenominators{} denominators and its two impact figures, gives \lttvCPEShareStated{} (table~\ref{tab:cpe-denominators}).

Responding to a question about the \$25 bundle, one month after the entry-level service launched, Morrison cited a much lower uptake figure than the report's: \enquote{the best estimates I've seen, Mr.~Waugh, are that about 4\% of Canadians will go for it} \citep[time marks 0920--0925]{commons2016chpc8}. He didn't say how it bore on the job estimate, or whether \enquote{4\% of Canadians} meant all Canadians, households or television subscribers.

\section{Comparing outcomes with the report's reform paths}
\label{sec:lttv-method}

The prediction record (forecasters, quantities, paths by year, stated assumptions) was committed before any CRTC outcome series was downloaded. I then re-read the report's two paths from the data labels on its charts, checking every value against the totals in its text, and ran a design analysis by fake-data simulation before opening any CRTC outcome file \citep{gelman2014types, gelman2020workflow}. It asked, for each forecast quantity, whether the outcome could separate a world in which the report's impact occurred from one in which it didn't, given that the baseline itself could be wrong. It separated the two worlds well for both revenue series and only weakly for CPE, so CPE was set aside in advance as descriptive (appendix~\ref{app:methods}).

Allowing for a wrong baseline is the hard part. In retrospective analysis of regulation, \enquote{developing a credible counterfactual is the most demanding aspect}, and the baselines assumed beforehand \enquote{must be revisited} to see whether outside factors changed the result \citep[286]{morgenstern2018retrospective}. Here the counterfactual is the report's own baseline, itself a forecast of how television would have fared under streaming without the reforms. So the check treats the baseline's error as unknown and reports results across a range of assumed scales for it. \textcite{kane2026sffa} varies the baseline period against which forecasts are judged; here the baseline is the report's own, and what varies is how wrong it's assumed to be.

For each revenue series I estimate a forecast scale \(k\). In logs, so that the forecast shortfall and the baseline's error are relative differences rather than dollar amounts, \(\log B_t-\log Y_t=k\,\delta_t+e_t\), where \(B_t\) is the report's baseline, \(Y_t\) the outcome, \(\delta_t\) the report's forecast shortfall in logs (\(\log B_t\) minus the log of the reform path) and \(e_t\) the baseline's error (positive when the baseline overstates what would have happened without the decisions), modelled as a random walk from 2014. So \(k=0\) corresponds to the baseline and \(k=1\) to the reform path, with baseline error in either case. I write \(\hat k\) for the estimate over 2016--2019, the four years before the pandemic.

Because the baseline's error accumulates from year to year, \(\hat k\) rests on changes in the gap between outcome and baseline rather than on its level: for specialty and pay revenue it's positive although that revenue stayed above the baseline in every year, because its excess over the baseline shrank, the direction the reform path predicted.

The 95\% interval for \(k\) reflects only the assumed error in the baseline, so its width depends on the annual error scale \(\sigma\), which is calibrated, not estimated from four years of outcomes, and treated as known. The interval also assumes the forecast impact is proportional to the drifted baseline. I also give 50\% intervals, which the true value should be as likely to fall inside as outside \citep[18]{gelmanHill2007}; the verdicts use the 95\% interval. Appendix~\ref{app:methods} gives the estimator and what these assumptions cost: in its illustration of uncertainty in \(\sigma\), the distributors' interval includes zero, and an impact fixed in dollars lowers coverage of \(k=1\) to \lttvCoverDollarsSpec{} and \lttvCoverDollarsBDU{} from 95\%.

The scale \(k\) compares the outcome with the report's two paths; it isn't an estimate of the decisions' causal effect, which would need a better counterfactual than the report's own baseline. The value of \(k\) for any other path is the estimate \(\hat k\) would take if revenue had followed that path exactly. The cited-input band is the range of such values for two paths built from the lowest and highest uptake estimates the report cites (appendix~\ref{app:methods}); it isn't a probability interval.

The plan's verdicts compare the 95\% interval with the band, in this order: \emph{inconclusive} if the interval contains both zero and the band's lower end; \emph{smaller} if it lies wholly below the band; \emph{exceeded} if it lies wholly above; otherwise \emph{consistent}.

The outcome series alone can't identify how wrong the baseline was, so the plan fixed an external check on \(\sigma\): the report's forecast of US Netflix subscribers, assumed unaffected by Canadian regulation, against Netflix's reported count (appendix~\ref{app:methods}). That check gives \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below the historical volatility of either revenue series, and the pre-stated rule takes the larger of the two, so the designated error scale is the historical volatility: \lttvSigmaReadSpec{} for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} for distributors' revenue.

\section{Revenue outcomes and their sensitivity to baseline error}
\label{sec:lttv-results}

\subsection{Against the report's paths}

The CRTC series reproduce the report's 2012--2014 values within \lttvSpliceTol{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}, and figure~\ref{fig:paths} shows each against the report's two paths. Specialty and pay revenue stayed above the report's baseline, by between \lttvSpecVsBaselineMin{} and \lttvSpecVsBaselineMax{} from 2016 to 2019, and ran between \lttvSpecVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvSpecVsLTTVMax{} \lttvSpecAboveLTTV{} the reform path. Taken alone, the revenue \lttvSpecRevNomDir{} \lttvSpecRevNomChange{} in nominal dollars from 2015 to 2019 and \lttvSpecRevRealChange{} after inflation, while the report's baseline was flat in nominal dollars over 2016--2019 (table~\ref{tab:inputs}).

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_paths.pdf}
\caption{Revenue relative to the report's baseline, 2012--2019, in per cent of the baseline. The reform path and the baseline are the report's (Figs.~41, 42); the partial recalculation holds BYOP uptake at the CRTC's June 2016 entry-level share and the exemption-order and closure dollar components fixed (post hoc); the outcome is the CRTC series (2016 edition to 2015, 2020 edition after; specialty and pay services exclude services exempt from individual licensing). The shaded ranges are the pointwise 95\% and 50\% ranges (the 50\% darker) around the baseline under the error model at the designated error scale (\lttvSigmaReadSpec{} and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} a year). Before 2015 the baseline is the report's own actual values. Both panels share one scale.}
\label{fig:paths}
\end{figure}

For specialty and pay revenue, at the designated error scale of \lttvSigmaReadSpec{}, \(\hat k=\lttvKSpec\), with a standard error of \lttvKSpecSE{}. That's \lttvKSpecSEsFromZero{} standard errors from \(k=0\) and \lttvKSpecSEsFromOne{} from \(k=1\), and the cited-input band's lower end, \lttvBandSpecLo{}, is \lttvKSpecSEsFromBandLo{} standard errors away. Under the pre-stated rule the verdict is \emph{smaller}: the 95\% interval, \lttvKSpecLoTwo{} to \lttvKSpecHiTwo{} (50\%: \lttvKSpecLoFifty{} to \lttvKSpecHiFifty{}), lies wholly below the band of \lttvBandSpecLo{} to \lttvBandSpecHi{}, so at this scale the outcome is incompatible with the reform path at any uptake the report cited.

Distributors' revenue ran between \lttvBDUVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvBDUVsLTTVMax{} \lttvBDUAboveLTTV{} the report's reform path, falling from \$\lttvBDURevFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvBDURevNineteen{} million in 2019, a nominal decline of \lttvBDURevNomChange{}, or \lttvBDURevRealChange{} after inflation. Here \(\hat k=\lttvKBDU\) (standard error \lttvKBDUSE{}), \lttvKBDUSEsFromZero{} standard errors from \(k=0\) and \lttvKBDUSEsFromOne{} from \(k=1\). Its interval, \lttvKBDULoTwo{} to \lttvKBDUHiTwo{} (50\%: \lttvKBDULoFifty{} to \lttvKBDUHiFifty{}), includes \(k=1\) and overlaps the band of \lttvBandBDULo{} to \lttvBandBDUHi{}, so under the pre-stated rule the verdict is \emph{consistent}.

\subsection{Uptake: the report's assumption and the evidence}

The report took its \lttvByopEighteen{} for 2018 onward from outside estimates, the highest being Oliver Wyman's finding that \enquote{as many as 35\% of subscribers would be willing to switch to a skinny-basic/BYOP option} \citep[para.~201, p.~75]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC counted more than \lttvUptakeAprilN{} subscribers to the entry-level package five weeks after launch \citep{crtc2016basicpackage} and \lttvUptakeJuneN{} by 30 June 2016 \citep[para.~12]{crtc2016hearing0907}, about \lttvUptakeAprilShare{} and \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} of the 2016 subscriber total. These count subscribers to the entry-level package with or without added channels, a different measure from the report's BYOP uptake, taken before every channel had to be offered singly as well as in small packages; I found no later CRTC count.

A survey by the Media Technology Monitor \citeyearpar{mtm2017starter}, released in August, put adoption of starter packages at \enquote{just over 1 in 10 TV subscribers} and, separately, reported that 29\% of subscribers were adding individual channels or bundles to their packages. Surveys aren't among the sources the analysis plan accepted for uptake. This one is self-reported, its release gives no fieldwork dates, sample size or margin of error, and it may not measure the report's BYOP share, so it's reported beside the planned reading. The survey path below reads its \enquote{just over 1 in 10} as 10\%, a floor, and assumes that level held from 2017 through 2019.

Low uptake in 2016 may partly reflect how the package was sold, a possibility the report itself raised, that distributors might offer unbundling in a way \enquote{relatively unattractive from a price-value equation, so that very few Canadians opt for it} \citep[para.~78, n.~40, p.~34]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's hearing of September 2016 examined \enquote{the practices certain providers have adopted in offering} it \citep[para.~5]{crtc2016hearing0907}. Uptake in mid-2016 was far below the report's 2016 assumption; whether it stayed low is what the survey puts in doubt.

\subsection{Partial recalculations under assumed uptake paths}

To ask what the report's chain implies at other uptake levels, I rescale each year's unbundling and preponderance components by the assumed BYOP share over the report's (Table~18) and hold the exemption-order and closure dollar components fixed. Since the report values the exemption-order and closure components partly from the other two \citep[paras.~220, 234]{nordicity2015television}, the recalculation is partial. Its scenario coefficient \(k^{u}\) is the value of \(\hat k\) that revenue following the recalculated path would give, and I call it compatible with the outcome when it lies inside the 95\% interval for \(k\). Table~\ref{tab:scenarios-main} shows four uptake paths, and table~\ref{tab:scenarios} all seven. The paths were added after the outcome data was opened, and the survey path uses a source outside the plan's (table~\ref{tab:chronology}).

\input{sections/table-scenarios-main}

With uptake held at the CRTC's June 2016 share, \(k^{u}=\lttvKPredSpecObsUptake\) for specialty and pay revenue, compatible with \(\hat k\) at the designated error scale (\lttvKPredSpecObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors away), and \lttvKPredBDUObsUptake{} for distributors, \lttvKPredBDUObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors below \(\hat k\), a gap that falls below two under any calibration with a larger error scale (section~\ref{sec:lttv-sensitivity}), with the CRTC series rescaled to the report's 2014 level (\lttvBDUGapSEsRescaled{}), and with the level offset of section~\ref{sec:lttv-modelcheck} (\lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{}). On the survey path, 1.6\% in 2016 and 10\% from 2017, \(k^{u}=\lttvKPredSpecSurvey\) for specialty and pay revenue, \lttvKPredSpecSurveySEs{} standard errors above \(\hat k\), though below the interval's upper end at the largest calibrated error scale, \lttvSigmaWidest{} (\lttvKSpecHiWidest{}), and \lttvKPredBDUSurvey{} for distributors, \lttvKPredBDUSurveySEs{} standard errors below. A linear rise from 1.6\% to \lttvMorrisonUptake{} by 2019 gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrison{} and \lttvKPredBDURiseMorrison{}, both inside their intervals. Among the paths tested, at the designated error scale, that rise is the only one that keeps both series compatible with the partial recalculation; larger error scales widen the set.

Even with uptake held at the June 2016 share, the scenario coefficients stay well above zero, because the exemption-order and closure components are held at the report's values.

\subsection{Distributors' revenue by subscribers and revenue per subscriber}

Splitting distributors' revenue into subscribers and revenue per subscriber shows where their shortfall against the report's baseline arose. The report's components act on different factors: unbundling lowers revenue per subscriber and leaves subscriber numbers alone, while the exemption order adds cord cutting, 1.9\% of subscribers a year against 1.5\% in the baseline \citep[paras.~204--205, 216, 220; Tables~5, 21]{nordicity2015television}. Rebuilding the report's exemption-order component from its stated cord cutting and cord shaving reproduces it to within about \lttvDecCheckMaxDev{} in every year, so the reform scenario's split can be recovered (table~\ref{tab:decomposition}).

The split is measured as changes from 2014, since in the report's actual years the CRTC's subscriber counts sit \lttvDecSubAlignLo{} to \lttvDecSubAlignHi{} below the report's and its revenue per subscriber \lttvDecPerAlignLo{} to \lttvDecPerAlignHi{} above. It assumes the two series stay comparable after 2014: the report's subscriber series includes \enquote{non-reporting BDUs} (Fig.~17; BDUs, broadcasting distribution undertakings, is the CRTC's term for distributors), the CRTC's cover broadcast years ending 31 August, and revenue per subscriber here is total distributor revenue, which is broader than a package price.

From 2014 to 2019 the CRTC's count of subscribers fell a further \lttvDecSubObs{} relative to the report's baseline path, against \lttvDecSubFc{} in its reform scenario, and revenue per subscriber fell \lttvDecPerObs{} relative to it, against \lttvDecPerFc{}: it rose only \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{} in nominal dollars, from \$\lttvRevPerSubFourteen{} a month in 2014 to \$\lttvRevPerSubNineteen{} in 2019 (\lttvRevPerSubRealFall{} lower after inflation), while the baseline path rose \lttvRevPerSubBaseGrowth{}; its underlying price assumption was inflation plus one point, before an allowance for cord shaving \citep[Table~11, paras.~151--152]{nordicity2015television}. In nominal terms distributors' revenue fell \lttvBDURevFallFourteenNineteen{} from 2014 to 2019, as subscribers fell \lttvSubsFallFourteenNineteen{} and revenue per subscriber rose \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{}; against the report's rising baseline, missing growth in revenue per subscriber accounts for about \lttvDecPerShare{} of the shortfall, in logs.

With uptake held at the June 2016 share, the partial recalculation gives a per-subscriber shortfall of \lttvDecPerCounted{}, and on the survey path \lttvDecPerSurvey{}. Measured in logs from 2014, the share of the total revenue shortfall that the recalculation leaves unexplained is \lttvDecBeyondCounted{} with uptake held at 1.6\% and \lttvDecBeyondSurvey{} on the survey path.

The revenue split was added after the outcome data was opened, under a rule fixed before it was computed (table~\ref{tab:chronology}); the comparisons with uptake held at 1.6\% and on the survey path go beyond that rule. It's an accounting identity, and revenue per subscriber is computed from the same totals, so the split locates the shortfall without observing prices or identifying causes. Subscriber losses exceed those in both of the report's paths compared here, and stagnant revenue per subscriber could reflect pricing, cord shaving to smaller packages, or the reforms themselves.

\subsection{Sensitivity to the error scale}
\label{sec:lttv-sensitivity}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_k_sigma.pdf}
\caption{The estimate \(\hat k\) and its 95\% and 50\% intervals (the 50\% darker) as a function of the annual error scale of the report's baseline, \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of the yearly changes in its error. The solid vertical line marks the designated error scale; dotted lines mark the values of \(\sigma\) used by the other calibrations (table~\ref{tab:calibrations}). The grey band is the cited-input band. The horizontal axis spans the plan's sensitivity range, 1\% to 8\% a year; intervals are conditional on \(\sigma\). The standard error is proportional to \(\sigma\), so the interval widens linearly while the estimate stays put.}
\label{fig:k-sigma}
\end{figure}

Both revenue series' intervals for \(k\) depend on the error scale (figure~\ref{fig:k-sigma}). The estimates don't move as the assumed scale increases; the intervals widen in proportion. The specialty and pay band starts well above the estimate because its lower end keeps the exemption-order and closure components at the report's values and scales only the uptake-driven ones; even with uptake held at the CRTC's June 2016 share, the partial recalculation gives \(k^{u}=\lttvKPredSpecObsUptake\) (table~\ref{tab:scenarios-main}). The specialty and pay interval reaches the cited-input band when the scale reaches about \lttvCutoffSpec{} a year, and at the largest calibrated scale, \lttvSigmaWidest{}, its upper end is \lttvKSpecHiWidest{}. The distributors' interval includes zero from about \lttvCutoffBDU{}. At the plan's upper value of 8\% a year, the specialty and pay interval, \lttvKSpecLoEight{} to \lttvKSpecHiEight{}, includes \(k=1\). None of the reported specialty and pay intervals excludes zero. The verdict labels in table~\ref{tab:calibrations} change as the assumed scale crosses these values while the estimate stays the same \citep{gelmanStern2006difference}. Every calibration other than the pre-stated one was added after the outcome data was opened, so all are shown \citep{gelman2014statcrisis}.

Other defensible readings of the Netflix comparison give larger scales: the 2016 miss gives a Netflix-derived scale of \lttvSigmaTechSixteen{} a year and a pooled estimate \lttvSigmaTechPooled{}. Part of the 2016 miss is an inherited offset, since the report's 2015 starting figure (\lttvNetflixFcFifteen{} million) was already above Netflix's count (\lttvNetflixObsFifteen{} million) \citep{netflix2018form10k}. Measured as growth, Netflix's memberships outran the Trefis forecast the report used, by \lttvNetflixObsGrowth{} against \lttvNetflixFcGrowth{} from 2015 to 2018, which gives a scale of \lttvSigmaGrowthEighteen{} a year.

Integrating over the error scale, instead of fixing it, gives a single interval that carries the uncertainty in \(\sigma\) (post hoc). Given \(\sigma\), \(k\) is normal about \(\hat k\), as in a regression whose variance matrix is known up to a scale \citep[372]{GelmanBDA3}. In the version specified before computing, the four years of residuals also bear on \(\sigma\), which the pre-stated reading doesn't allow. With a uniform prior on the plan's range of 1\% to 8\% a year, the specialty and pay 95\% interval then runs from \lttvKIntSpecUnifLo{} to \lttvKIntSpecUnifHi{}, just below the band's lower end of \lttvBandSpecLo{}, and the distributors' from \lttvKIntBDUUnifLo{} to \lttvKIntBDUUnifHi{}; the posterior medians of \(\sigma\) are \lttvKIntSpecUnifSigmaMed{} and \lttvKIntBDUUnifSigmaMed{}. Treating the report's 2010--2014 volatility as data gives \lttvKIntSpecHistLo{} to \lttvKIntSpecHistHi{} and \lttvKIntBDUHistLo{} to \lttvKIntBDUHistHi{}. Both verdicts match those at the designated scale, the specialty and pay one narrowly under the uniform prior. With \(\sigma\) set by the prior alone, a version computed after that one, the result depends on the prior. The uniform prior, which puts as much weight on 8\% a year as on 2\%, gives \lttvKIntSpecUnifOnlyLo{} to \lttvKIntSpecUnifOnlyHi{} and \lttvKIntBDUUnifOnlyLo{} to \lttvKIntBDUUnifOnlyHi{}, both inconclusive. The history-based prior gives \lttvKIntSpecHistOnlyLo{} to \lttvKIntSpecHistOnlyHi{} for specialty and pay, still \emph{smaller}, and \lttvKIntBDUHistOnlyLo{} to \lttvKIntBDUHistOnlyHi{} for distributors, an interval that reaches zero and so is inconclusive (table~\ref{tab:calibrations}; appendix~\ref{app:methods}).

\subsection{Checking the error model}
\label{sec:lttv-modelcheck}

A check of the statistical error model, added after the outcome data was opened, finds the specialty and pay residual concentrated in the change from 2014 to 2016. After fitting \(k\), the estimated changes in the baseline's error between observations, scaled by \(\sigma\), are correlated and have variances below one, because the fit uses up part of the variation. Divided by its own standard deviation under the fit, the specialty and pay change from 2014 to 2016 is \lttvInnovSpecFirst{}, and the largest of the three later changes is \lttvInnovSpecLaterMax{} in absolute value; the distributors' changes show no such pattern. A one-time gap between the report's baseline and the CRTC series would produce this, though with four points so would a random walk whose later steps happened to be small.

Part of specialty and pay revenue's excess over the report's baseline is already visible in 2015, a year with no forecast impact, in the report's own figure for that year (itself a forecast). The CRTC later counted \$\lttvCRTCFifteenSpec{} million, \lttvGapFifteenSpec{} \lttvGapFifteenSpecDir{} the report's \$\lttvReportFifteenSpec{} million, against \lttvGapFourteenSpec{} in 2014 and negligible differences in 2012 and 2013, when the report's figures were actuals. Distributors' revenue shows no such change: the CRTC's counts run between \lttvGapRangeLoBDU{} and \lttvGapRangeHiBDU{} \lttvGapFifteenBDUDir{} the report's figures in every year from 2012 to 2015, a standing difference between the two series, with no new divergence in 2015.

The 2016 and 2020 editions of the CRTC's summaries differ on 2016 by \lttvReleaseGapSpec{} for specialty and pay services and \lttvReleaseGapBDU{} for distributors, so revisions between editions can't account for the gap. Allowing a level offset in the error model, which absorbs a one-time gap of this kind and the distributors' standing difference, gives \(\hat k=\lttvKSpecOffset\) (standard error \lttvKSpecOffsetSE{}) for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvKBDUOffset{} (\lttvKBDUOffsetSE{}) for distributors' revenue, leaving both pre-stated verdicts as they were; the distributors' comparison with uptake held at 1.6\% falls to \lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{} standard errors.

\section{Payments, closures and staff counts}
\label{sec:lttv-links}

\subsection{Payments to Canadian channels}

The report also assumed a path for what distributors pay Canadian channels. In its baseline the monthly carriage fee per subscriber for Canadian specialty and pay services rises \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{} from 2015 to 2019 \citep[Table~14, p.~67]{nordicity2015television}, and under the decisions it falls below that path as distributors pass on \lttvReportPassThrough{} of the retail loss attributed to Canadian services. What distributors paid Canadian channels in affiliation payments rose from \$\lttvPayCanFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvPayCanNineteen{} million in 2019 while subscribers fell, so per subscriber it rose \lttvPerSubGrowth{}, and the Canadian share of all affiliation payments stayed near \lttvPayShareFifteen{} \citep[Table~U-T11]{crtc2019cmrbdu}. After inflation the total \lttvPayCanRealDir{} \lttvPayCanRealChange{} and the payment per subscriber \lttvPerSubRealDir{} \lttvPerSubRealChange{}; the comparison with the report's fee path needs no such adjustment, since that path is nominal too.

The report's fee is the average monthly amount Canadian specialty, pay, pay-per-view and video-on-demand services earn per subscriber \citep[para.~180, Table~14]{nordicity2015television}; the CRTC series is what distributors report paying all Canadian affiliates, divided by distributors' subscribers. The two differ in who reports them, in which services they cover and possibly in the subscriber base, so their growth is compared, not their levels. With uptake near the CRTC's 2016 share there would have been little loss to pass on, and the comparison would mainly show that payments grew faster than the report's baseline assumed; on the survey path, the partial recalculation has fees falling relative to the baseline path, and observed payments instead grew faster than it.

The aggregates can't say what fees would have been without the decisions, or why affiliation payments per subscriber rose. One structural model shows how renegotiation can offset the fee revenue channels lose when subscribers drop them. Simulating mandatory à la carte in the US, a far larger change than the CRTC's, \textcite[644, 676--678]{crawford2012bundling} find that channels' licence-fee revenue would fall by half if fees stayed at their bundled levels, but by only 3.7\% once contracts between channels and distributors are renegotiated, when the per-subscriber fees summed over the channels rise 103\%. That model predicts a small fall, not the rise observed here, and the aggregates can't show which mechanism operated. Some of the payments stay inside the integrated groups, and the report itself expected the exemption order's impact on those groups to be partly offset by their streaming and broadband revenue \citep[para.~227, p.~83]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's wholesale code, which \enquote{governs the commercial relationship between BDUs and programmers} and was scheduled to take effect in January 2016 \citep[p.~72, n.~80; p.~73, n.~82]{nordicity2015television}, is in both of the report's scenarios, so it can't account for the difference unless its effect exceeded what the report assumed.

\subsection{Closures and programming expenditure}

The plan classifies each channel by its 2015 owner. That puts the \lttvShawMediaN{} specialty channels Shaw Media operated before its transfer to Corus, approved in March 2016, with the integrated companies, and Corus's own channels with the independents \citep{crtc2016chart32h, crtc2016chart32i, crtc2016decision110}. On that classification, \lttvClosVIPlanClosed{} to \lttvClosVIPlanUpper{} of the integrated companies' \lttvClosVIPlanN{} Category A and B channels stopped operating by 2019--2020 (\lttvClosVIPlanLo{} to \lttvClosVIPlanHi{}), slightly below the report's \lttvReportClosuresVI{}, which implies about \lttvClosVIPlanImplied{}, a difference of two or three channels. The report's footnote 31, citing the CRTC, lists Shaw/Corus as one vertically integrated entity \citep[n.~31]{nordicity2015television}, and the CRTC regards the two as under the same effective control \citep{crtc2016decision110}; counting Corus as integrated, as the plan also required showing, gives \lttvClosVICorusClosed{} to \lttvClosVICorusUpper{} of \lttvClosVICorusN{} (\lttvClosVICorusLo{} to \lttvClosVICorusHi{}), around the \lttvClosVICorusImplied{} that the report's rate implies.

For the independents the bounds, \lttvClosIndPlanClosed{} to \lttvClosIndPlanUpper{} of \lttvClosIndPlanN{} (\lttvClosIndPlanLo{} to \lttvClosIndPlanHi{}) on the plan's classification and \lttvClosIndCorusLo{} to \lttvClosIndCorusHi{} with Corus integrated, contain the report's \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} but are too wide to test it, because in the summaries used here channels that continued under an exemption from individual licensing can't be told apart from channels that closed.

CPE, read only descriptively, ran between \$\lttvCPEObsMin{} million and \$\lttvCPEObsMax{} million a year from 2016 to 2019, above the report's baseline path of \$\lttvCPEBaseMin{} million to \$\lttvCPEBaseMax{} million.

\subsection{Staff counts}

For specialty and pay services and for distributors, the CRTC's staff counts allow a descriptive comparison with the last link in the chain, from revenue to jobs \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}. The report gives its forecast changes in direct employment by sector against a baseline whose employment path it doesn't publish, so the comparison is with the change from 2015 and with the 2012--2015 trend carried forward, a crude stand-in for that baseline. Specialty and pay services' staff fell from \lttvStaffChanFifteen{} in 2015 to \lttvStaffChanNineteen{} in 2019, \lttvStaffChanVsTrend{} \lttvStaffChanVsTrendDir{} the trend, against a forecast shortfall in direct employment of \lttvStaffChanForecast{} FTEs by 2019. Distributors' staff stayed near its 2012--2015 trend, \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteen{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteenDir{} it in 2018 and \lttvStaffDistVsTrend{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendDir{} it in 2019, against a forecast shortfall of \lttvStaffDistForecast{} FTEs by 2019 \citep[Table~22, p.~91]{nordicity2015television}. The 2019 figure is a one-year jump that reverses the next year, which may be a reporting discontinuity.

Measured against these benchmarks, staff and revenue point in opposite directions in both sectors, which the report's chain doesn't imply: specialty and pay services cut staff below trend while their revenue stayed above the report's baseline, and distributors' staffing stayed near trend while their revenue fell below the baseline (annual series in table~\ref{tab:staff}). The mismatch can't test the report's employment prediction: staff counts aren't the report's modelled FTEs; the distributor series is labelled \enquote{Total Staff Count (FTE)} in the 2016 edition and \enquote{Total Staff Count} in the 2020 edition, and the two differ by \lttvStaffDistVintageGap{} in 2016; and a straight-line trend is a weak counterfactual. The direction of the mismatch holds with the distributors' 2018 figure in place of 2019.
